rows.subtopic: Electric Dipole and Dipole in a Uniform Field
rows.stem: An electric dipole of dipole moment \(1{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-12}\) Cm lies along x-axis. An electric field of magnitude \(2{\cdot}0 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{NC^{-1}}\) is switched on at an instant in the region. The unit vector along the electric field is \(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\hat{i} + \dfrac{1}{2}\hat{j}\). The magnitude of the torque acting on the dipole at that instant is :
rows.solution:
**The answer is (B): \(1{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-8}\) Nm.**

**The torque on a dipole in a uniform field.**

\(\vec{\tau} = \vec{p}\times\vec{E} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \tau = pE\sin\theta\)

where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\vec{p}\) and \(\vec{E}\). So the only real work is **finding that angle**.

**Reading the angle off the unit vector.**

\(\hat{E} = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\hat{i} + \dfrac{1}{2}\hat{j}\)

*(A check that it is genuinely a unit vector: \(\left(\sqrt{3}/2\right)^{2} + \left(1/2\right)^{2} = \tfrac{3}{4} + \tfrac{1}{4} = 1\ \checkmark\))*

Its components are \(\left(\cos\theta, \sin\theta\right)\) with

\(\cos\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \qquad \sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \theta = 30^\circ\)

and since the dipole lies along the \(x\)-axis, \(30^\circ\) is exactly the angle between \(\vec{p}\) and \(\vec{E}\).

**Substituting.**

\(\tau = \left(1{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-12}\right)\left(2{\cdot}0 \times 10^{4}\right)\sin 30^\circ = \left(2{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-8}\right) \times \dfrac{1}{2}\)

\(\boxed{\ \tau = 1{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{Nm}\ }\)

**Option (C) is the answer with \(\sin\theta\) left out** — that is, \(pE\) alone, which would be the torque only if the dipole were perpendicular to the field. Option (D) doubles it, which is what \(\sin\theta = 2\) would give and is impossible. The whole question is whether the \(30^\circ\) is spotted and its sine used.

**Note which component supplies the torque.** It is the **\(\hat{j}\)** component of \(\vec{E}\), the one **perpendicular** to the dipole, that does the turning; the \(\hat{i}\) component is parallel to \(\vec{p}\) and exerts no torque at all. That is why the answer contains the \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) and not the \(\sqrt{3}/2\) — a useful cross-check on which trigonometric function belongs.

**Why the word "at that instant" appears.** A free dipole would immediately begin to rotate towards alignment, and as \(\theta\) shrinks so does the torque, reaching zero at \(\theta = 0\). The value computed is the torque at the moment the field is switched on, when the dipole is still along \(x\).

**And why there is no net FORCE.** The field is uniform, so the forces \(+q\vec{E}\) and \(-q\vec{E}\) on the two ends are equal and opposite — they form a pure **couple**. The dipole turns on the spot without being dragged anywhere, which is what makes a dipole in a uniform field the cleanest case in electrostatics.

rows.stem: When the switch of the circuit is turned on, the filament of the bulb glows instantaneously because :

options.label: A
options.text: the electrons coming from the power source move fast through the initially empty filament.

options.label: B
options.text: the filament may be old having low resistance.

options.label: C
options.text: electric field is established instantaneously across the filament which pushes the electrons.

options.label: D
options.text: free electrons in the filament travel with the speed of light.

rows.solution:
**The answer is (C): an electric field is established almost instantaneously across the filament, which pushes the electrons.**

**The apparent puzzle.** Electrons in a metal drift extraordinarily slowly — at around \(10^{-4}\) m/s, a fraction of a millimetre per second. At that rate an electron leaving the switch would take **hours** to reach the bulb. Yet the bulb lights the instant the switch closes.

**The resolution: nothing has to travel from the switch to the bulb.**

When the circuit is completed, the **electric field** propagates along the conductor at a speed close to that of light — of order \(10^{8}\) m/s. Within nanoseconds a field is established throughout the whole circuit, including the filament.

**That field acts on the electrons ALREADY IN the filament**, which have been sitting there all along. They all begin drifting at once, everywhere in the circuit simultaneously, and a current flows through the filament immediately. The filament heats, and it glows.

**The analogy that makes it concrete.** A long pipe already full of water: open the tap and water flows from the far end at once, not after the new water has travelled the length of the pipe. The **pressure** travels fast; the water itself moves slowly. Here the field is the pressure and the electrons are the water.

**Why the other three fail.**

**(A)** claims electrons come from the power source through an "initially empty" filament. The filament is a **metal**, crammed with some \(10^{28}\) free electrons per cubic metre; it is never empty, and no electron needs to arrive from anywhere.

**(B)** blames a low resistance from age. A **lower** resistance would make it glow *brighter*, not sooner — and in fact a filament's resistance **rises** as it ages and thins. This confuses brightness with delay.

**(D)** says the electrons travel at the speed of light. They emphatically do not: their **drift** speed is \(\sim 10^{-4}\) m/s and even their random thermal speed is only \(\sim 10^{5}\) m/s. What moves near \(c\) is the **field**, not the charge.

**The distinction worth carrying away.** Three quite different speeds live in the same wire — the **drift** speed \(\left(10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m/s}\right)\), the random **thermal** speed \(\left(10^{5}\ \mathrm{m/s}\right)\) and the speed at which the **signal**, meaning the field, propagates \(\left(\sim 10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s}\right)\). Almost every puzzle about "how fast is electricity" dissolves once these are kept apart.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem: A particle with charge q moving with velocity \(\vec{v} = v_0\hat{i}\) enters a region with magnetic field \(\vec{B} = B_1\hat{j} + B_2\hat{k}\). The magnitude of force experienced by the particle is :
rows.solution:
**The answer is (C): \(qv_0\sqrt{B_1^{2} + B_2^{2}}\).**

**The quickest route: notice that \(\vec{B}\) has NO component along \(\vec{v}\).**

The velocity is along \(\hat{i}\), and

\(\vec{B} = B_1\hat{j} + B_2\hat{k}\)

contains no \(\hat{i}\) term at all. So \(\vec{B}\) is **entirely perpendicular** to \(\vec{v}\), the angle between them is \(90^\circ\), and

\(F = qvB\sin 90^\circ = qv_0\left|\vec{B}\right| = qv_0\sqrt{B_1^{2} + B_2^{2}}\)

\(\boxed{\ F = qv_0\sqrt{B_1^{2} + B_2^{2}}\ }\)

**The same result by working the cross product out**, which also gives the direction:

\(\vec{F} = q\left(\vec{v}\times\vec{B}\right) = q\left[v_0\hat{i}\times\left(B_1\hat{j} + B_2\hat{k}\right)\right]\)

Using \(\hat{i}\times\hat{j} = \hat{k}\) and \(\hat{i}\times\hat{k} = -\hat{j}\):

\(\vec{F} = qv_0\left(B_1\hat{k} - B_2\hat{j}\right)\)

\(\left|\vec{F}\right| = qv_0\sqrt{B_1^{2} + B_2^{2}}\ \checkmark\)

**Why the components add in QUADRATURE, not directly.** \(B_1\) and \(B_2\) are components of one vector along **perpendicular** axes, so the field's magnitude is \(\sqrt{B_1^{2} + B_2^{2}}\), never \(B_1 + B_2\). Option (A) makes exactly that error, and it is the one the question is built to catch.

**Options (B) and (D) fail on DIMENSIONS**, without any physics. Both place \(v_0\) **inside** a square root together with the field, giving \(\sqrt{\text{velocity} \times \text{field}}\) — a quantity with no meaningful units, and certainly not newtons. Two of the four options can therefore be discarded by inspection.

**A useful check on the direction.** The force \(qv_0\left(B_1\hat{k} - B_2\hat{j}\right)\) has no \(\hat{i}\) component, so it is perpendicular to \(\vec{v}\) — as a magnetic force always must be. It is also perpendicular to \(\vec{B}\): their dot product is \(qv_0\left(B_1B_2 - B_2B_1\right) = 0\). Both checks are free and catch most cross-product slips.

**What the particle will actually do.** With \(\vec{v}\) entirely perpendicular to \(\vec{B}\), the path is a **circle** in the plane perpendicular to \(\vec{B}\), of radius \(r = mv_0\big/q\sqrt{B_1^{2} + B_2^{2}}\). Had \(\vec{B}\) carried an \(\hat{i}\) component, that part of the velocity would have been unaffected and the path would have been a helix instead.

rows.stem: The materials having negative magnetic susceptibility are :
rows.solution:
**The answer is (A): diamagnetic.**

**What susceptibility measures.** The magnetic susceptibility \(\chi\) relates the magnetisation a material acquires to the field applied:

\(\vec{M} = \chi\vec{H}\)

A **negative** \(\chi\) means the magnetisation points **opposite** to the applied field — the material magnetises *against* the field.

**That is the defining property of a diamagnetic substance.** It has no permanent magnetic moment (all electrons paired), so when a field is applied the orbital motion of its electrons is perturbed to induce a moment **opposing** the field — Lenz's law acting at the atomic scale.

**The three classes by susceptibility.**

| Class | \(\chi\) | Typical size | \(\mu_r = 1 + \chi\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Diamagnetic** | **NEGATIVE** | \(-10^{-5}\) | slightly **less** than 1 |
| Paramagnetic | positive, small | \(+10^{-5}\) | slightly more than 1 |
| Ferromagnetic | positive, **large** | \(10^{3}\) to \(10^{5}\) | very much greater than 1 |

**The range is bounded below by \(-1\).** Since \(\mu_r = 1 + \chi\) cannot be negative, \(\chi \ge -1\); and \(\chi = -1\) exactly would mean the material excludes the field **completely**, which is what a **superconductor** does. A superconductor is thus the perfect diamagnet, and the Meissner effect is diamagnetism taken to its limit.

**Why option (D) is not a real answer.** "Non-magnetic" is not one of the three classes. **Every** substance responds to a magnetic field in one of the three ways above; what is loosely called non-magnetic simply means not ferromagnetic, and such a material is still either diamagnetic or paramagnetic.

**The consequence of a negative \(\chi\).** A diamagnetic sample is **repelled** by a magnet — pushed towards the weaker field — whereas paramagnetic and ferromagnetic materials are drawn in. Bismuth, copper, water, glass and most organic matter are diamagnetic; the effect is faint, but in a strong field it is unmistakable, and water's diamagnetism is enough to levitate a frog in \(16\) T.

**And note that diamagnetism is universal.** The induced opposing moment arises in every substance. A material is *called* diamagnetic only when there is no permanent moment to swamp it — which is exactly the case when all the electrons are paired.

rows.stem: When current in a coil changes at a steady rate from 8 A to 6 A in 4 ms, an emf of \(1{\cdot}5\) V is induced in it. The value of self-inductance of the coil is :
rows.solution:
**The answer is (C): 3 mH.**

**Self-induction.**

\(\left|\varepsilon\right| = L\left|\dfrac{dI}{dt}\right| \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad L = \dfrac{\left|\varepsilon\right|}{\left|dI/dt\right|}\)

**Compute the rate of change**, converting the milliseconds:

\(\left|\dfrac{dI}{dt}\right| = \dfrac{8 - 6}{4 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{2}{4 \times 10^{-3}} = 500\ \mathrm{A\,s^{-1}}\)

**The "ms" is the whole arithmetic.** Reading \(4\) ms as \(4\) s would give \(0{\cdot}5\) A/s and an inductance of \(3\) H — a thousand times too large, and a value no small coil could have.

**Substituting.**

\(L = \dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{500} = 3 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{H}\)

\(\boxed{\ L = 3\ \mathrm{mH}\ }\)

**The word "steadily" matters.** It guarantees \(dI/dt\) is **constant** over the interval, so a single number describes the whole \(4\) ms and the induced emf is steady at \(1{\cdot}5\) V throughout. Without it, \(dI/dt\) would be an instantaneous quantity and the question would have no unique answer.

**The current DECREASES, but the answer does not care.** The change \(8 \to 6\) A is a fall, so strictly \(dI/dt = -500\) A/s and the induced emf opposes the decrease — it acts to keep the current flowing. But inductance is a positive property of the coil, and the magnitudes are what is asked for. (That the emf opposes the *change*, not the current, is Lenz's law: here it tries to sustain the current, not to kill it.)

**What self-inductance is, physically.** \(L\) measures how much flux the coil links **with its own** current, \(N\phi = LI\). A coil with large \(L\) resists changes in its current strongly, which is why an inductor is called a **choke** — and why breaking a circuit containing one produces a sharp voltage spike and often a visible spark.

**A sense of the value.** \(3\) mH is a very ordinary small inductor — a few hundred turns on a small core. Note how modest an emf it takes: \(1{\cdot}5\) V, about a cell's worth, from a current change of just \(2\) A. But compress that same change into a **microsecond** instead of \(4\) ms and the emf would be \(6000\) V, which is exactly how an ignition coil works.

rows.stem: The electric field in space between the plates of a parallel plate capacitor (each of area \(2{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m^2}\)) is changing at the rate of \(4 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{Vm^{-1}s^{-1}}\). The displacement current between the plates of the capacitor is :
rows.solution:
**The answer is (C): \(8{\cdot}85 \times 10^{-8}\) A.**

**Maxwell's displacement current.**

\(i_d = \varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\phi_E}{dt}\)

With a uniform field \(E\) over a plate area \(A\), the electric flux is \(\phi_E = EA\), and since the area is fixed:

\(i_d = \varepsilon_0 A\dfrac{dE}{dt}\)

**Substituting**, with \(\varepsilon_0 = 8{\cdot}85 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{C^{2}N^{-1}m^{-2}}\):

\(i_d = \left(8{\cdot}85 \times 10^{-12}\right)\left(2{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-3}\right)\left(4 \times 10^{6}\right)\)

**Take the two given numbers first**, since they multiply to a clean power of ten:

\(\left(2{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-3}\right)\left(4 \times 10^{6}\right) = 1{\cdot}0 \times 10^{4}\)

\(i_d = 8{\cdot}85 \times 10^{-12} \times 1{\cdot}0 \times 10^{4}\)

\(\boxed{\ i_d = 8{\cdot}85 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{A}\ }\)

**The mantissa is \(\varepsilon_0\)'s own**, which is the signature of the right answer and a quick way to recognise it among the options — the rest of the calculation contributes only the exponent.

**Why a "current" flows where no charge does.** Nothing crosses the gap between the plates: it is a vacuum or a dielectric, with no free carriers. What flows is the **consequence** of a changing electric field, which Maxwell showed produces a magnetic field exactly as a real current does. It is a current in its magnetic effect, not in its mechanism.

**Where the term came from.** Ampere's law applied to a charging capacitor gives two different answers for the same loop, depending on whether the chosen surface cuts the **wire** (enclosing the conduction current) or passes **between the plates** (enclosing none). Adding \(i_d\) removes the contradiction, because between the plates

\(E = \dfrac{q}{\varepsilon_0 A} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad i_d = \varepsilon_0 A\dfrac{dE}{dt} = \dfrac{dq}{dt} = i_c\)

**The displacement current exactly equals the conduction current in the wires** — the \(\varepsilon_0\) and the \(A\) cancel completely — so the total current is continuous all the way round the circuit.

**And what it led to.** Because a changing electric field makes a magnetic field, and a changing magnetic field makes an electric one, the two can sustain each other with no charges present at all. That is the electromagnetic wave — and hence light — which is why this one extra term is arguably the most consequential addition in classical physics.

rows.stem: In a double slit experiment, the two slits are \(1{\cdot}5\) mm apart. The slits are illuminated by a mixture of lights of wavelengths of 600 nm and 400 nm and the interference pattern is observed on a screen \(1{\cdot}5\) m away from the slits. Find the minimum distance of the point from the central maximum at which bright fringes of the interference patterns of the two wavelengths coincide.
rows.solution:
**When do fringes of two wavelengths coincide?**

Bright fringes lie at

\(y_n = \dfrac{n\lambda D}{d}\)

so the \(n_1\)th fringe of \(\lambda_1\) falls on the \(n_2\)th fringe of \(\lambda_2\) when the **positions** match — and since \(D\) and \(d\) are common,

\(n_1\lambda_1 = n_2\lambda_2\)

**Find the smallest whole numbers that satisfy it.**

\(n_1\left(600\right) = n_2\left(400\right) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dfrac{n_1}{n_2} = \dfrac{400}{600} = \dfrac{2}{3}\)

**The smallest integer pair is \(n_1 = 2\), \(n_2 = 3\).** Both orders must be whole numbers — a fringe of order \(1{\cdot}5\) does not exist — which is what forces the ratio into lowest terms.

*(Excluding the trivial \(n_1 = n_2 = 0\), which is the central maximum itself: there **all** wavelengths coincide, since the path difference is zero for every colour. The question asks for the first coincidence **away** from it.)*

**The position.**

\(y = \dfrac{n_1\lambda_1 D}{d} = \dfrac{2 \times 600 \times 10^{-9} \times 1{\cdot}5}{1{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-3}}\)

\(\boxed{\ y = 1{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m} = 1{\cdot}2\ \mathrm{mm}\ }\)

**Check it with the other wavelength**, which must give the same place:

\(y = \dfrac{3 \times 400 \times 10^{-9} \times 1{\cdot}5}{1{\cdot}5 \times 10^{-3}} = 1{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m}\ \checkmark\)

**This check is worth doing every time**, because it tests both the orders and the arithmetic at once, and it uses the half of the data the first calculation ignored.

**What is actually seen on the screen.** The two wavelengths produce two interleaved fringe patterns of different spacings — \(\beta_1 = 0{\cdot}6\) mm for the \(600\) nm light and \(\beta_2 = 0{\cdot}4\) mm for the \(400\) nm. Between the centre and \(1{\cdot}2\) mm they fall out of step, and the screen shows a confusion of red and blue maxima. At \(1{\cdot}2\) mm they line up again and a bright fringe of **both** colours appears, then the cycle repeats every \(1{\cdot}2\) mm.

**The general rule.** Coincidences recur at multiples of the **lowest common multiple** of the two fringe widths: \(\mathrm{LCM}\left(0{\cdot}6, 0{\cdot}4\right) = 1{\cdot}2\) mm. Reading the answer that way makes it a single line, and makes clear why \(1{\cdot}2\) mm is a *spacing* and not just a position.

rows.subtopic: Refraction at Spherical Surfaces and by Lenses
rows.stem: Find the focal length of plano-convex lens of refractive index \(1{\cdot}5\) and radius of curvature 10 cm when it is immersed in a liquid of refractive index \(1{\cdot}25\).
rows.solution:
**The lens-maker's formula for a lens in a surrounding medium.**

\(\dfrac{1}{f} = \left(\dfrac{n_{\text{lens}}}{n_{\text{medium}}} - 1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2}\right)\)

**The ratio \(n_{\text{lens}}/n_{\text{medium}}\) is the RELATIVE refractive index**, and using it in place of \(n\) is the whole adaptation needed for an immersed lens.

**The radii of a plano-convex lens.** One face is curved with radius \(R = 10\) cm; the other is **plane**, which is a sphere of infinite radius:

\(R_1 = 10\ \mathrm{cm}, \qquad R_2 = \infty\)

\(\dfrac{1}{R_1} - \dfrac{1}{R_2} = \dfrac{1}{10} - 0 = \dfrac{1}{10}\)

**Substituting.**

\(\dfrac{1}{f} = \left(\dfrac{1{\cdot}5}{1{\cdot}25} - 1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{10}\right) = \left(1{\cdot}2 - 1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{10}\right) = \dfrac{0{\cdot}2}{10} = \dfrac{1}{50}\)

\(\boxed{\ f = 50\ \mathrm{cm}\ }\)

**The numbers are chosen so that \(1{\cdot}5/1{\cdot}25 = 1{\cdot}2\) exactly**, which keeps the whole calculation to one line.

**Compare with the focal length in AIR.**

\(\dfrac{1}{f_{\text{air}}} = \left(1{\cdot}5 - 1\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{10}\right) = \dfrac{1}{20} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad f_{\text{air}} = 20\ \mathrm{cm}\)

**So immersion makes this lens two and a half times weaker** — \(20\) cm becomes \(50\) cm. The glass has not changed at all; only what surrounds it has.

**Why the lens weakens.** Refraction depends on the **contrast** between the two media at each surface. In air the contrast is \(1{\cdot}5\) against \(1{\cdot}0\); in the liquid it is \(1{\cdot}5\) against \(1{\cdot}25\), a much smaller step, so each surface bends the light far less.

**The two limits worth knowing.** If the liquid had \(n = 1{\cdot}5\), the bracket would **vanish**, \(f\) would be infinite, and the lens would be optically **invisible** — neither converging nor diverging. And if the liquid were **denser** than the glass, the bracket would go negative and this convex lens would **diverge**.

**Why the plane face contributes nothing.** With \(R_2 = \infty\), the term \(1/R_2\) is zero: a flat surface has no curvature and so no focusing power. All the convergence of a plano-convex lens comes from its one curved face, which is why its focal length is twice that of an equiconvex lens of the same radius and material.

rows.subtopic: Line Spectra of the Hydrogen Atom
rows.stem: Find the ratio of minimum to maximum wavelength of radiations emitted when electron jumps from higher energy state into ground state of hydrogen atom.
rows.solution:
**Which series is this?** Transitions ending on the **ground state** \(\left(n_f = 1\right)\) form the **Lyman series**. So both the shortest and the longest wavelength must be found within that series.

**The Rydberg formula.**

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R\left[\dfrac{1}{n_f^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{n_i^{2}}\right] \qquad\text{with}\ n_f = 1\)

**The MINIMUM wavelength** corresponds to the **largest** energy jump, which comes from \(n_i = \infty\) — the series limit:

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda_{\min}} = R\left[\dfrac{1}{1} - \dfrac{1}{\infty}\right] = R \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \lambda_{\min} = \dfrac{1}{R}\)

**The MAXIMUM wavelength** corresponds to the **smallest** jump that still lands on \(n = 1\), which is from \(n_i = 2\):

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda_{\max}} = R\left[\dfrac{1}{1} - \dfrac{1}{4}\right] = \dfrac{3R}{4} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \lambda_{\max} = \dfrac{4}{3R}\)

**The ratio**, in which the Rydberg constant cancels:

\(\dfrac{\lambda_{\min}}{\lambda_{\max}} = \dfrac{1/R}{4/3R} = \dfrac{3}{4}\)

\(\boxed{\ \lambda_{\min} : \lambda_{\max} = 3 : 4\ }\)

**The inversion is the thing to keep straight.** The **largest** energy gap gives the **shortest** wavelength, since \(\lambda = hc/\Delta E\). So \(\lambda_{\min}\) belongs to \(\infty \to 1\) and \(\lambda_{\max}\) to \(2 \to 1\) — the opposite pairing to the one the words might suggest.

**The same result through energies**, which needs no Rydberg constant at all:

\(\Delta E_{\max} = 0 - \left(-13{\cdot}6\right) = 13{\cdot}6\ \mathrm{eV} \quad\text{for}\ \infty \to 1\)

\(\Delta E_{\min} = -3{\cdot}4 - \left(-13{\cdot}6\right) = 10{\cdot}2\ \mathrm{eV} \quad\text{for}\ 2 \to 1\)

\(\dfrac{\lambda_{\min}}{\lambda_{\max}} = \dfrac{\Delta E_{\min}}{\Delta E_{\max}} = \dfrac{10{\cdot}2}{13{\cdot}6} = \dfrac{3}{4}\ \checkmark\)

**The actual wavelengths**, for orientation. With \(R = 1{\cdot}097 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}\):

\(\lambda_{\min} = 91\ \mathrm{nm}, \qquad \lambda_{\max} = 122\ \mathrm{nm}\)

**Both are deep in the ultraviolet**, and necessarily so: any transition to \(n = 1\) must supply at least \(10{\cdot}2\) eV, far above the \(1{\cdot}8\) to \(3{\cdot}1\) eV the eye can see. That is why the Lyman series is invisible, and why the **Balmer** series — ending on \(n = 2\) — is the one that gives hydrogen its familiar visible lines.

**How narrow the whole series is.** The entire Lyman series is squeezed between \(91\) and \(122\) nm, a ratio of only \(3:4\), because the levels above \(n = 1\) crowd together so tightly compared with the vast gap below them.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Force and Motion in a Magnetic Field
rows.stem:
(a) A charged particle q moving with a velocity \(\vec{v}\) is subjected to a uniform magnetic field \(\vec{B}\) acting perpendicular to \(\vec{v}\). If a uniform electric field \(\vec{E}\) is also set up in the region along the direction of \(\vec{B}\), describe the path followed by the particle and draw its shape.
(b) How will the magnetic field inside a long solenoid be affected when :
(i) the radius of the turns of the solenoid is increased,
(ii) the length of solenoid as well as the total number of its turns are doubled ?
rows.solution:
**(a) The path of the particle.**

**Set it up by splitting the motion.** Take \(\vec{B}\) along the \(z\)-axis; the electric field is stated to be along \(\vec{B}\), so \(\vec{E}\) is along \(z\) too, and \(\vec{v}\) is initially perpendicular to both, say along \(x\).

**The MAGNETIC force acts only in the perpendicular plane.** \(\vec{F}_B = q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}\) is perpendicular to \(\vec{v}\) and to \(\vec{B}\), so it lies in the \(xy\) plane and produces **uniform circular motion** there, of radius

\(r = \dfrac{mv_\perp}{qB}\)

**The ELECTRIC force acts only along the axis.** \(\vec{F}_E = q\vec{E}\) is along \(z\), parallel to \(\vec{B}\), so it produces a **uniform acceleration** along the axis:

\(a = \dfrac{qE}{m}\)

**The two are completely independent**, since each acts along a direction the other does not touch. Superposing them:

\(\boxed{\ \text{A HELIX with constant radius but CONTINUOUSLY INCREASING pitch}\ }\)

*The shape to draw:* a coil wound about the direction of \(\vec{B}\), its loops all the **same width** but spaced further and further apart as the particle advances — a spring being stretched along its axis.

**Why the radius stays constant while the pitch grows.** The electric force adds speed only along \(z\), and the radius \(r = mv_\perp/qB\) depends on the **perpendicular** component alone, which the electric field never touches and the magnetic force cannot change (it does no work). But the axial speed climbs steadily, so in each successive revolution — and the period \(T = 2\pi m/qB\) is the **same** every time — the particle advances further:

\(\text{pitch} = v_z T \quad\text{with } v_z \text{ increasing}\)

**Contrast with the two simpler cases.** With no electric field, \(v_z\) would be constant and the helix would have **uniform** pitch. With \(\vec{v}\) entirely perpendicular and no \(\vec{E}\), the path would close into a **circle**. The stretching helix is what the added axial force produces.

**(b) The field inside a long solenoid.**

\(B = \mu_0 nI = \mu_0\left(\dfrac{N}{l}\right)I\)

**(i) The radius of the turns is increased.**

\(\boxed{\ \text{NO CHANGE}\ }\)

**The radius does not appear in the formula at all.** The field inside a long solenoid depends only on the turns **per unit length** and the current — not on how wide the coil is. Widening it spreads the same field over a larger cross-section, so the **flux** \(\left(\phi = B\pi r^{2}\right)\) rises, but the field itself does not.

**(ii) The length and the total number of turns are both doubled.**

\(n' = \dfrac{2N}{2l} = \dfrac{N}{l} = n\)

\(\boxed{\ \text{NO CHANGE}\ }\)

**It is the RATIO that matters, not either quantity alone.** Doubling both leaves the turns per unit length untouched — the winding is just as tightly packed as before, over twice the length — so the field is identical.

**What the two parts together are testing.** \(B = \mu_0 nI\) contains **no** geometric quantity except \(n\). Neither the radius, nor the length, nor the total turn count can change the field on its own; only \(N/l\) and \(I\) can. Both changes here are deliberately chosen to leave \(n\) alone.

rows.stem:
(a) Differentiate between magnetic flux through an area and magnetic field at a point.
(b) A bar magnet is held with its length along the axis of a closed coil. Initially the south pole of the magnet faces the coil. If the magnet is moved towards the coil, explain how a current is induced in the coil and in what direction.
rows.solution:
**(a) Magnetic flux through an area, against magnetic field at a point.**

| | **Magnetic field \(\vec{B}\)** | **Magnetic flux \(\phi\)** |
|---|---|---|
| What it describes | a **POINT** in space | an **AREA** or surface |
| Nature | a **vector** | a **scalar** |
| Definition | force per unit charge per unit velocity, from \(\vec{F} = q\vec{v}\times\vec{B}\) | \(\phi = \int\vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A} = BA\cos\theta\) for a uniform field |
| SI unit | **tesla** (T), or \(\mathrm{Wb\,m^{-2}}\) | **weber** (Wb) |
| Picture | how densely the field lines are packed **there** | the total **number** of field lines crossing the surface |

**The relation between them.** Flux is the field **integrated over a surface**, so it depends not only on how strong the field is but on how big the area is and how it is **tilted**. The same field gives maximum flux through an area held perpendicular to it \(\left(\theta = 0\right)\) and **zero** flux through the same area turned edge-on \(\left(\theta = 90^\circ\right)\), even though the field has not changed at all.

**Why the distinction is worth insisting on.** Faraday's law involves \(d\phi/dt\), not \(dB/dt\) — so an emf can be induced with the field held perfectly **constant**, simply by rotating or resizing the coil. That is precisely how an AC generator works, and it is unintelligible if flux and field are conflated.

**(b) The bar magnet approaching the coil, south pole first.**

**Step 1 — the flux through the coil increases.** As the south pole comes nearer, the magnet's field at the coil grows stronger, so more field lines thread it. *(Field lines run **into** a south pole, so the flux through the coil is directed **towards** the magnet — but what matters is only that its magnitude is increasing.)*

**Step 2 — so an emf, and a current, are induced.** By Faraday's law,

\(\varepsilon = -\dfrac{d\phi}{dt}\)

and since the coil is **closed**, that emf drives a current round it.

**Step 3 — Lenz's law fixes the direction.** The induced current opposes the **change** that produced it, so it must oppose the magnet's **approach** — which means the coil must **repel** the incoming south pole.

**To repel a south pole, the near face of the coil must itself become a SOUTH pole**, since like poles repel.

**Step 4 — from pole to current sense.** Using the clock rule: viewed from outside, a face behaves as a **south** pole when the current in it runs **clockwise**.

\(\boxed{\ \text{The induced current is CLOCKWISE, seen from the magnet's side}\ }\)

**The energy account, which is the real content of Lenz's law.** The coil pushes back on the magnet, so whoever is moving it must do **work** against that repulsion — and that work is what appears as electrical energy dissipated in the coil's resistance. Were the current to flow the other way, the coil would **attract** the magnet, pulling it in faster, inducing more current, and energy would be created from nothing.

**And what happens if the magnet is pulled AWAY instead.** The flux now **decreases**, the induced current reverses, the near face becomes a **north** pole, and the coil **attracts** the retreating magnet — again opposing the change, and again requiring work to be done.

rows.subtopic: Refraction and Reflection of Plane Waves
rows.stem:
(a) Define 'wavefront' of a light wave. A plane wavefront is refracted from a convex lens. Draw the shape of the refracted wavefront.
(b) A plane wave travelling in a medium is incident on a plane surface separating this medium from a rarer medium. Draw a diagram to show refraction of the wave. Hence, verify Snell's law.
rows.solution:
**(a) Wavefront, and the shape after a convex lens.**

**Definition.** A **wavefront** is the locus of all points of a wave that are vibrating **in the same phase** — a surface of constant phase. Its shape depends on the source: a point source gives **spherical** wavefronts, and at a great distance from the source a small portion of such a sphere is effectively **plane**.

**A plane wavefront refracted by a convex lens.**

\(\boxed{\ \text{It emerges as a CONVERGING SPHERICAL wavefront}\ }\)

*To draw it:* a series of vertical straight lines (the plane wavefront) arriving at the lens from the left, and to the right of the lens a series of **arcs curving towards a point** — the focus — with their concave sides facing forward and shrinking as they approach \(F\).

**Why it becomes spherical.** The lens is **thickest at its centre**, so light passing through the middle is slowed the most, while light through the thin edges is delayed least. The central part of the wavefront therefore falls **behind** the edges, and a flat surface is bent into one curving forward towards a point. After the focus the wavefronts expand again as diverging spheres.

**(b) Refraction of a plane wave from a denser into a rarer medium, and Snell's law.**

**The construction.** Let a plane wavefront \(AB\) in the denser medium (speed \(v_1\)) strike the plane interface \(XY\), reaching \(A\) first and \(C\) last. Draw the normal at \(A\) and let the angle of incidence be \(i\), the angle of refraction \(r\).

*Diagram:* interface \(XY\) horizontal; the incident wavefront \(AB\) meeting it at \(A\), with \(BC\) perpendicular from \(B\) to the surface at \(C\); a wavelet of radius \(AE\) drawn in the rarer medium below, and the tangent \(CE\) from \(C\) to it as the refracted wavefront. Because the medium below is **rarer**, \(v_2 > v_1\) and the wavelet is **larger** than \(BC\) — so the refracted wavefront tilts the other way and the ray bends **away** from the normal.

**Huygens' principle**: every point on a wavefront is a source of secondary wavelets, and the new wavefront is the surface touching them all.

**Step 1.** Let \(t\) be the time for the disturbance to travel from \(B\) to \(C\), still in the first medium:

\(BC = v_1t\)

**Step 2.** In that **same** time \(t\), the wavelet that started from \(A\) the instant the wavefront arrived has spread into the second medium to a radius

\(AE = v_2t\)

**The equality of the two times is the whole proof** — both describe the one interval \(t\).

**Step 3.** Draw the tangent \(CE\) from \(C\) to that wavelet: it is the refracted wavefront.

**Step 4 — the geometry.** In the right-angled triangles \(ABC\) and \(AEC\), which share the hypotenuse \(AC\):

\(\sin i = \dfrac{BC}{AC} = \dfrac{v_1t}{AC}, \qquad \sin r = \dfrac{AE}{AC} = \dfrac{v_2t}{AC}\)

**Step 5 — divide.** Both \(AC\) and \(t\) cancel:

\(\dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{v_1}{v_2}\)

and with \(n = c/v\),

\(\boxed{\ \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1}, \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad n_1\sin i = n_2\sin r\ }\)

which is **Snell's law**.

**Reading the denser-to-rarer case.** Here \(n_1 > n_2\), so \(\sin r > \sin i\) and \(r > i\): the ray bends **away** from the normal, as the larger wavelet in the diagram shows. Push \(i\) up far enough and \(\sin r\) would exceed \(1\) — impossible — and at that point no refracted wavefront can be constructed at all. That is the **critical angle**, and beyond it the light is **totally internally reflected**; the Huygens construction shows exactly why it happens only in this direction.

**What the construction explains that the formula alone does not.** Refraction is not a force acting on a ray but the geometric consequence of one edge of the wavefront entering the new medium before the other and changing speed there. The wavefront pivots — like a column of marchers turning when those on one flank lengthen their stride.
